human_review: The bookkeeper decides how to fix each batch or deposit that does not match, and a person sends any missing or corrected thank-you letter the agents drafted.
The treasurer checks each giving statement before it goes out and decides about gifts with no giver or no date; statements and letters are sent by a person.
A person merges duplicate records in the CRM, recodes gifts, claims employer matches and answers card disputes; the agents never change the CRM, refund or charge a card.
The finance lead confirms the fair market value of each benefit and the disclosure wording; the volunteer coordinator decides on background checks and the hours that count.
The grants manager decides on cost transfers, drawdown requests and report submissions, and talks to the auditor about the single audit; nothing is drawn or submitted by the agents.
The controller decides on releases, transfers and the endowment draw, and the board approves designations; the agents prepare draft entries and post nothing.
The preparer or auditor reviews the Form 990 data, the 1099 list and the functional split before anything is filed; the agents file nothing.
Every finding in every pack goes to a named person, who decides and acts; the agents only read files and write reports and drafts.
Each client's own staff act on its findings, and the firm confirms each client's settings (fiscal year, thresholds, spending policy) with the client.
common_problems: Gift batches deposited short or never deposited, and contribution revenue in the ledger that does not match the CRM.
Gifts over 250 with no thank-you letter, a late letter, a wrong amount or no goods-or-services statement.
Gala and event payments receipted as fully deductible when the donor received a dinner or another benefit.
Gifts whose note names a restricted purpose coded to general operating, and restricted funds spent below zero.
Restricted money spent and never released, or released before its date or beyond what was spent.
Grant budget lines over budget, costs dated outside the award period, and indirect costs charged on more than the allowed base.
Pledges 90 days or more past due, and conditional pledges kept open as receivables.
Duplicate donor records that share an e-mail, a phone number or an address.
reaches_the_model: When an assistant calls a tool, its model sees the result: amounts, dates, rates, finding codes, record ids (donor, gift, employee and volunteer ids) and text such as fund, grant and account names in clear. Donor, member, volunteer, staff, officer and vendor names, e-mails, phone numbers, street addresses and taxpayer ids are replaced by tokens such as M.H.#eb764c (checked with 261 fictional values in 22 agents, 0 leaks). Memos, notes and bank descriptions are sent as typed, so a name written only there reaches the model. The report and draft files written on your computer keep the real values. Results go to whatever model your assistant uses; for donor and staff data, use a model covered by your own agreements or a local model.
rules_maintained: Every rule that changes with the law, a funder or your own policy is a setting, not code: the acknowledgement and quid pro quo thresholds and the IRS's yearly insubstantial-benefit figures, the single audit threshold and the de minimis indirect rate (both chosen by fiscal year or award date), the 1099 threshold (by tax year), the Form 990 schedule thresholds, appraisal and disposal periods, endowment spending and prudence rates, and your own receipt, mileage, per diem and background-check rules. Defaults live in each agent's src/logic.js, with the source and date in the review. Your values go in a settings JSON file merged over the defaults, and every result lists the settings it used. You change the file yourself, or support updates it when a figure changes.
